The '''Lwów school of mathematics''' ({{langx|pl|Lwowska szkoła matematyczna}}) was a group of Polish [[mathematician]]s who worked in the [[interwar period]] in [[Lwów]], [[Second Polish Republic|Poland]] (since 1945 [[Lviv]], [[Ukraine]]). The mathematicians often met at the famous [[Scottish Café]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mauldin |first=R. Daniel |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-22897-6 |title=The Scottish Book: Mathematics from The Scottish Café, with Selected Problems from The New Scottish Book |date=2015 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-319-22896-9 |location=Cham |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-22897-6}}</ref> to discuss mathematical problems, and published in the journal ''[[Studia Mathematica]]'', founded in 1929. The school was renowned for its productivity and its extensive contributions to subjects such as [[point-set topology]], [[set theory]] and [[functional analysis]]. 

==Members==
Notable members of the Lwów school of mathematics included:
{{Div col|colwidth=20em}}
* [[Stefan Banach]]
* [[Feliks Barański]]
* [[Władysław Orlicz]]
* [[Stanisław Saks]]
* [[Hugo Steinhaus]]
* [[Stanisław Mazur]]
* [[Stanisław Ulam]]
* [[Józef Schreier]]
* [[Juliusz Schauder]]
* [[Mark Kac]]
* [[Antoni Łomnicki]]
* [[Stefan Kaczmarz]]
* [[Herman Auerbach]]
* [[Włodzimierz Stożek]]
* [[Stanisław Ruziewicz]]
* [[Eustachy Żyliński]]
{{Div col end}}The biographies and contributions of these mathematicians were documented in 1980 by their contemporary, [[Kazimierz Kuratowski]] in his book ''A Half Century of Polish Mathematics: Remembrances and Reflections''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kuratowski |first=Kazimierz |title=A half century of polish mathematics: remembrances and reflections |last2=Kirkor |first2=Andrzej |last3=Kuratowski |first3=Kazimierz |date=1980 |publisher=Pergamon Pr. [usw.] |isbn=978-0-08-023046-7 |series=International series of monographs on pure and applied mathematics |location=Oxford [usw.] Frankfurt}}</ref>

==The end of the school==
First the [[Soviet annexation of Eastern Galicia and Volhynia]] in 1939, then the [[Operation Barbarossa|German invasion of the Soviet Union]] in 1941, caused many of the mathematicians to flee Lwów. Few of them survived [[World War II]], but after the war a group including some of the original community carried on their work in [[Wrocław]] in Silesia, after the [[Polish population transfers (1944–1946)|post-war Polish population transfers]]. A number of the prewar mathematicians, prominent among them [[Stanisław Ulam]], became famous for work done in the [[United States]].
